claims.claim: Garcia read and compared more than 5,500 pages of D&D and Pathfinder rulebook text across editions for his 2017 study.
claims.source: Antero Garcia, Mind, Culture, and Activity 24(3), 2017

claims.claim: The 1989 AD&D second edition defended its exclusive male pronoun as clear, concise and familiar in written material.
claims.source: David 'Zeb' Cook, AD&D 2nd ed. (1989) p. 9, quoted by Antero Garcia (2017)
claims.page: Gender construction and representation in D&D, p. 238

claims.claim: Garcia reports that D&D rulebooks stopped explaining their pronoun choice from the third edition (2000) onward.
claims.source: Antero Garcia, Mind, Culture, and Activity 24(3), 2017
claims.quote: Explanations about pronouns would cease with later editions

claims.claim: The 5e Player's Handbook tells the reader that nine human ethnic groups are widely recognized in the Forgotten Realms.
claims.source: D&D 5e Player's Handbook (2014) p. 30, quoted by Antero Garcia (2017)
claims.quote: nine human ethnic groups are widely recognized

claims.claim: The same 5e passage frames material culture and physical characteristics as varying by region.
claims.source: D&D 5e Player's Handbook (2014) p. 30, quoted by Antero Garcia (2017)
claims.quote: change wildly from region to region

claims.claim: The 5e half-orc entry carries a bolded named paragraph, 'Grudging Acceptance', describing how half-orcs are received by others.
claims.source: D&D 5e Player's Handbook (2014) p. 41, quoted by Antero Garcia (2017)

claims.claim: Gygax described Holmes's contribution to the 1977 Basic Set as the rewriting and editing that extracted a beginner's set from existing D&D texts.
claims.source: Gary Gygax, Dragon #14 (May 1978), compiled by Zach Howard, Zenopus Archives, 2013
claims.quote: the rewriting and editing necessary to extract a

claims.claim: Gygax said TSR decided the original booklets needed a clarified introductory piece for a wider readership.
claims.source: Gary Gygax, Dragon #35 (March 1980), compiled by Zach Howard, Zenopus Archives, 2013

claims.claim: An RPGA interviewer in 1981 characterised Holmes's Basic Set as easier reading than the original set and Mentzer's as understandable by anyone willing to read it.
claims.source: RPGA interviewer (presumed Frank Mentzer), Polyhedron #1 (1981), compiled by Zach Howard

claims.claim: Gygax judged Holmes's editorial work on the Basic Set favourably in a 2005 forum reply.
claims.source: Gary Gygax, EN World post 22 Feb 2005, compiled by Zach Howard
claims.quote: fine bit of editing with the set

claims.claim: Trammell argues the aim of the orientalist register is encyclopedic knowledge of an imagined other.
claims.source: Aaron Trammell, Analog Game Studies III:1, January 2016
claims.quote: produce encyclopedic knowledge about an imagined and exotic other
claims.page: image caption, section on Orientalist texts

claims.claim: Trammell criticises the reductionism by which one sourcebook is written as if a whole culture could be contained by a single text.
claims.source: Aaron Trammell, Analog Game Studies III:1, January 2016

claims.claim: Trammell shows Oriental Adventures gives elite occupations far more specific named detail than commoner ones.
claims.source: Aaron Trammell, Analog Game Studies III:1, January 2016
claims.quote: the culture of the common people is barely distinguishable

claims.claim: A reader commenting on Trammell's essay attributes Oriental Adventures' authorship to David Cook on the evidence of its diction and style.
claims.source: Commenter on Aaron Trammell, Analog Game Studies, comment thread
claims.quote: Judging from the diction and style of the writing

claims.claim: Merwin advises putting information useful to the DM but not for players into an appendix.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Outlines and Frameworks', D&D Beyond, 9 Oct 2019
claims.quote: not meant to be seen by the players
